sources.title: Wikipedia GeoSearch, downtown Atlanta (33.7550, -84.3880, 2.5 km radius)
National Register of Historic Places listings in Fulton County, Georgia

stops.name: Woodruff Park
stops.description: Six acres of lawn, fountain and pavilion wedged between Peachtree Street and Park Place, given to the city anonymously in 1971 by Coca-Cola's Robert Woodruff, whose name only went on it fourteen years later.

stops.name: Five Points Monument
stops.description: A 36-foot bronze and steel tower raised for the 1996 Olympics at the intersection that gave downtown its name, built as a deconstructed water tower pulled apart and reassembled.

stops.name: William-Oliver Building
stops.description: Atlanta's first finished Art Deco skyscraper, put up in 1930 at Five Points and now carved into 115 apartments.

stops.name: Flatiron Building
stops.description: A wedge-shaped 1897 tower on the Peachtree and Broad split that predates its far more famous New York namesake by five years.

stops.name: Healey Building
stops.description: A 1913 Gothic Revival tower around a skylit atrium, planned as twin towers until the First World War killed the second half, making it the last of Atlanta's pre-war skyscraper boom.

stops.name: Rialto Center for the Arts
stops.description: A movie house has stood on this Forsyth Street site since 1916; the current 833-seat hall is run by Georgia State University and hosts the National Black Arts Festival.

stops.name: Statue of Henry W. Grady
stops.description: Unveiled in 1891 at Marietta and Forsyth to honor the Atlanta Constitution editor who sold the country on a New South, and contested ever since over what else he stood for.

stops.name: Candler Building
stops.description: Coca-Cola founder Asa Candler's 1906 marble-clad tower, the tallest building in Georgia when it opened and a hotel today.

stops.name: Ellis Hotel
stops.description: Opened in 1913 as the Winecoff and advertised as fireproof, it burned on December 7, 1946 killing 119 people, the deadliest hotel fire in American history and the reason modern fire codes look the way they do.

stops.name: Hurt Building
stops.description: An 18-story triangular wedge built between 1913 and 1926, one of the country's earliest skyscrapers and the first home of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.

stops.name: Atlanta Constitution Building
stops.description: The 1947 newspaper plant Ralph McGill wrote from, empty for decades above the railroad gulch and added to the National Register in January 2026.

stops.name: Georgia State Capitol
stops.description: A National Historic Landmark finished in 1889 and topped with a dome gilded in leaf hauled down from north Georgia's own gold country.

stops.name: Atlanta City Hall
stops.description: The city's fourth city hall, a 1930 neo-Gothic tower on the block where Sherman's staff ran occupied Atlanta in 1864.

stops.name: Central Presbyterian Church
stops.description: Founded in 1858 and occupied by Union troops six years later, this congregation still faces the Capitol across Washington Street.

stops.name: Shrine of the Immaculate Conception
stops.address: 48 Martin Luther King Jr Dr SW
stops.description: Atlanta's oldest standing church building, finished in 1873, whose predecessor was spared the burning of the city when its priest talked the Union command out of it.

note: Atlanta had never been scouted; it wins outright over the seven cities in the log (Cleveland, Denver, Boston, Dallas, Detroit, Green Bay, Houston). 15 stops verified, all with an English Wikipedia article and coordinates. The cluster is one walkable loop: Peachtree Street from Woodruff Park north to the Ellis Hotel, back down Forsyth, then south into Capitol Hill - roughly 1.2 miles end to end. Every street address was confirmed against the Fulton County NRHP listings or the article infobox, then run through Nominatim for the ZIP; 11 of 15 came back with the building itself named in the match (Healey Building, Rialto, Candler, Ellis Hotel, Hurt Building, the Capitol, Central Presbyterian, the Shrine), which is a strong confirmation. Note the Capitol carries its own ZIP, 30334, not the 30303 of everything around it. THREE STOPS HAVE NO ADDRESS AND THEREFORE NO ZIP, all deliberately: Woodruff Park (Wikipedia gives none, and 91 Peachtree St NE - the address usually quoted for it - resolved ambiguously to both 30308 and 30303 in the Hotel District block north of the park, so it was not worth guessing), the Five Points Monument (a plaza installation at an intersection) and the Grady statue (stands in the Marietta and Forsyth roadway). DROPPED: the Atlanta Zero Mile Post, which reads as a perfect stop and is not one - the original stone was moved to the Atlanta History Center in Buckhead in 2018 and only a replica plus an interpretive marker stands downtown; a human may still want it, but it is no longer the artifact the article is about. Also dropped: Atlanta from the Ashes (The Phoenix), which is a fine sculpture but sits inside Woodruff Park and would be a second stop at the first stop; and the whole Sweet Auburn cluster - Big Bethel AME, the APEX Museum, the Odd Fellows Building, the Prince Hall Masonic Temple, Ebenezer Baptist and the MLK National Historical Park - which is a mile east of Five Points and deserves its own separate walk rather than being bolted onto this one. Sweet Auburn is the obvious second Atlanta batch.
